title: Hello World
intro: Our first program prints a line. Put this in src/main.rs and run cargo run.

coming_from.go: `fn main` in `src/main.rs` is your `func main` in `package main`, and `println!` is closest to `fmt.Printf` with the `\n` added: the first argument is a format string, so `fmt.Println("x =", x)` becomes `println!("x = {x}")`. `cargo run` is `go run`, and `Cargo.toml` is where `go.mod`'s name and requirements go. The `!` means a macro, which lets the compiler check the format string while it builds.
coming_from.kotlin: `fn main` and `println!` read just like Kotlin's `fun main` and `println`. The `!` marks a macro, and `cargo run` builds a native executable: there is no JVM and no jar to run it.
coming_from.python: `println!` is your `print`, but its first argument is a format string, not a list of values: `print("x =", x)` becomes `println!("x = {x}")`. Code can't sit at the top level of the file: everything starts from `fn main`, with no `if __name__ == "__main__"`. `cargo run` compiles the program first, then runs it.
coming_from.typescript: `println!` is your `console.log`, but its first argument is a format string, not a list of values: `console.log("x =", x)` becomes `println!("x = {x}")`. The `!` marks a macro. There is no `node` or `tsc` step: `cargo run` compiles a native executable and runs that, and `Cargo.toml` plays the part of `package.json`.
coming_from.java: `fn main()` is your `public static void main(String[] args)`. Java 25 lets a single-file program drop the class and `static`, and Rust never had either: `main` is a free function and Rust has no classes. `println!` is a macro, not a method, so the compiler checks the format string and its arguments before the program runs.
coming_from.csharp: `fn main()` is your `static void Main`, written out: Rust has no top-level statements, so every statement must be inside a function. `println!` is `Console.WriteLine`, and the `!` marks a macro that checks the `{}` placeholders against the arguments at build time.
coming_from.c: `fn main()` is `int main(void)` and `println!` is `printf` with the `\n` added for you. A wrong or missing argument for a `{}` is a compile error, where a wrong `printf` argument is undefined behaviour, and there is no `return 0` to write.
coming_from.cpp: `println!` plays the role of `std::cout << ... << "\n"`, with `{}` placeholders like C++20 `std::format`. Like `std::format`, a bad format string or a missing argument fails to compile. `main` has no `return 0` and no `int`.

notes: `fn main()` is where the program starts. It takes no parameters and, by default, returns nothing. Nothing outside a function runs: a `println!` at the top of the file is an error.
`println!` writes a line to standard output; `eprintln!` writes to standard error. The `!` marks a macro: [Macros, attributes, naming](/learn/macros-attributes-naming/) has the format-string syntax.
`cargo new hello` makes a project, `cargo run` builds and runs it, and `cargo check` only looks for errors, which is faster. The executable lands in `target/debug/`.

gotcha.title: Giving main a return value
gotcha.looks_fine: In C and C++, `main` returns an `int` and the program ends with `return 0`. C# lets `Main` return an `int` too.
gotcha.rust_sees: `main` may return `()`, a `Result`, or an `ExitCode`. An `i32` is none of those, so the compiler says `main` has an invalid return type and suggests `()` or a `Result`.
gotcha.why: Rust's `main` can return anything that implements the `Termination` trait, and that trait decides the exit code. `()` means success, so most programs return nothing. To pick a code, return `std::process::ExitCode`; to fail with a message, return a `Result` (the lesson shows both). A bare number is not accepted, so the code cannot come from a stray value.

go.says: Go refuses: "func main must have no arguments and no return values". To set an exit code, call `os.Exit(n)`.
go.error:
# command-line-arguments
./main.go:5:6: func main must have no arguments and no return values

kotlin.says: Kotlin compiles `fun main(): Int`, but built with `kotlinc -include-runtime` the jar has no entry point and `java -jar` fails with "no main manifest attribute". Kotlin's `main` returns nothing; call `exitProcess(n)` to choose a code.
kotlin.out: no main manifest attribute, in main.jar

python.says: Python has no `main` to return from: the file runs from the top. The exit code comes from `sys.exit(n)`.

typescript.says: TypeScript has no `main` either. Set `process.exitCode = n`, or call `process.exit(n)`.

java.says: `public static int main` compiles, then the JVM reports "Main method not found in class Main" and exits with 1. Java's `main` must return `void`; call `System.exit(n)`.

csharp.says: C# accepts this: a top-level `return 0;` (or an `int` return from `Main`) sets the exit code. Rust gets the same result with `ExitCode`.

c.says: This is plain C: `main` returns an `int`, and 0 means success. In Rust the equivalent is `ExitCode`, and returning `()` already means 0.

cpp.says: This is plain C++: `main` returns an `int`, and `return 0` may be left out because the compiler adds it. Rust's equivalent is `ExitCode`.

error[E0277]: `main` has invalid return type `i32`
 --> src/main.rs:1:14
  |
1 | fn main() -> i32 {
  |              ^^^ `main` can only return types that implement `Termination`
  |
  = help: consider using `()`, or a `Result`
